title: The Narrow Ground
text: At Thermopylae in 480 BCE, a small Greek force defended a narrow route against a much larger Persian army. The position reduced the advantage of numbers, but it could not guarantee victory. The battle became legendary; careful history separates later patriotic storytelling from evidence about the campaign.
context: A non-graphic summary emphasizing terrain and source criticism.
vocabulary: terrain: the physical features of land
patriotic: expressing devotion to one's country
source: Original summary based on Herodotus and modern scholarship

references.citation: Original summary based on Herodotus and modern scholarship

title: The Double Envelopment
text: At Cannae, Hannibal arranged his troops so the Roman advance pressed into the Carthaginian center. Stronger wings then moved around the crowded formation. The result became a famous study in encirclement. Strategy students also remember its human warning: elegant diagrams represent real fear, loss, and consequence.
context: A non-graphic explanation of the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE.
vocabulary: encirclement: surrounding from all sides
formation: an organized arrangement

title: Mud, Distance, and Discipline
text: At Agincourt in 1415, English archers faced a larger French force on constricted, muddy ground. Long-range arrows disrupted the advance, while crowding reduced movement. Historians debate exact numbers and causes. The battle shows why weather, terrain, equipment, and command must be studied together.
context: A concise and non-graphic analysis of a medieval battle.
vocabulary: constricted: made narrow
disrupted: interrupted the order of
source: Original historical summary based on modern scholarship

references.citation: Original historical summary based on modern scholarship

title: The Straits of Salamis
text: Themistocles persuaded the Greek alliance to fight the Persian fleet in the narrow waters near Salamis. Restricted space made the larger fleet harder to coordinate. Victory depended on ships and rowers, but also on intelligence, persuasion, and choosing the place of decision before the enemy did.
context: A strategic overview of the naval battle of 480 BCE.
vocabulary: strait: a narrow water passage
coordinate: organize parts to work together

title: Waterloo and the Coalition
text: Waterloo was not simply a duel between two famous commanders. Wellington's allied army held its position while Prussian forces approached, and Napoleon struggled to defeat them separately. The campaign shows how timing and cooperation shape outcomes. Leadership matters, but armies, logistics, allies, and chance matter too.
context: A balanced, non-graphic account of the 1815 campaign.
vocabulary: coalition: a temporary alliance
logistics: movement and supply of forces

title: Information at Midway
text: Before the Battle of Midway, American codebreakers helped identify the Japanese objective. Commanders used incomplete intelligence to position their carriers. The victory changed the Pacific War, but uncertainty remained throughout the battle. Good information improves decisions; it never removes risk or guarantees a result.
context: A non-graphic summary of intelligence and decision-making in 1942.
vocabulary: intelligence: analyzed information
objective: a goal or target

title: The Open Ground at Gaugamela
text: In 331 BCE, Alexander met Darius III near Gaugamela. The Persian king chose and prepared broad ground for his larger army and chariots. Alexander advanced at an angle, drawing part of the Persian line away from its center. When a gap appeared, his cavalry drove toward it. The victory depended on trained units and coordination, not on one dramatic charge alone. It ended Darius's effective rule but did not end resistance to Alexander.
context: A concise tactical account that avoids reducing Gaugamela to a lone hero's action.
vocabulary: coordination: organized action by different groups
cavalry: soldiers who fight on horseback
source: Original summary based on Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Gaugamela

title: The Ridge at Hastings
text: In 1066, Harold's English army formed a shield wall on high ground near Hastings. William of Normandy attacked with archers, foot soldiers, and cavalry. The long battle changed as some English fighters pursued retreating Normans and opened gaps. Harold was killed, although later stories disagree about exactly how. William's victory led to conquest, land seizures, and a new ruling elite. Terrain and discipline mattered, but so did the strain of a battle lasting most of a day.
context: A source-aware overview of the Battle of Hastings and its consequences.
vocabulary: shield wall: a close defensive line of overlapping shields
elite: a group holding unusual power or privilege
source: Original summary based on English Heritage, The Battle of Hastings

references.citation: English Heritage, The Battle of Hastings

title: Mist and Heights at Austerlitz
text: At Austerlitz in 1805, Napoleon appeared to weaken his right side and encouraged a larger Allied army to attack there. Russian and Austrian forces moved down from the Pratzen Heights, thinning their center. French troops then emerged through morning mist and seized the heights, splitting the Allied position. The plan was daring, but its success also required accurate timing, experienced soldiers, and mistakes by opposing commanders. The victory reshaped European alliances for a time; it did not create permanent peace or make later campaigns inevitable.
context: A tactical explanation of Austerlitz that includes uncertainty and longer consequences.
vocabulary: alliance: an agreement to cooperate
inevitable: certain to happen
source: Original summary based on Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Austerlitz

title: Three Days at Gettysburg
text: The Battle of Gettysburg in July 1863 was not planned by either army at that exact place. Roads brought Union and Confederate forces together, and nearby ridges became crucial defensive ground. Fighting shifted from north of town to Cemetery Hill, Little Round Top, and finally the open field crossed during Pickett's Charge. Union lines held. The battle caused enormous loss on both sides and ended Lee's invasion of the North, but the Civil War continued for nearly two years. Gettysburg mattered through geography, command choices, endurance, and consequences—not through a single moment alone.
context: A non-graphic overview of Gettysburg's sequence, terrain, and significance.
vocabulary: defensive: intended to resist an attack
invasion: an armed entry into another region
source: Original summary based on U.S. National Park Service, Battle Detail: Gettysburg

references.citation: U.S. National Park Service, Battle Detail: Gettysburg

title: The Siege of Tenochtitlan
text: In 1521, Spanish forces led by Hernán Cortés and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies besieged the Mexica capital of Tenochtitlan. Brigantines contested the lake while attackers advanced along causeways and cut supplies. Smallpox, introduced earlier from Europe, had badly weakened the city's population. Calling the struggle simply a Spanish victory hides the central role of Tlaxcalans and other peoples with their own reasons for opposing Mexica power. The city's fall brought destruction and colonial rule, but Indigenous communities continued to shape Mexico. Strategy, disease, alliances, and unequal consequences all belong in the explanation.
context: A multi-causal account centered on Indigenous alliances as well as Spanish weapons and disease.
vocabulary: besieged: surrounded to cut off supplies
causeway: a raised road across water or low ground
source: Original summary based on Smithsonian Institution, Mexican America: History

title: Supply and Resolve at Imphal and Kohima
text: In 1944, Japanese forces advanced from Burma toward the British bases at Imphal and Kohima in northeast India. British, Indian, Gurkha, and African units defended the region while aircraft delivered food, ammunition, and reinforcements. Japanese troops had expected to capture Allied supplies, so the stalled offensive left them dangerously short of food and medicine during the monsoon. Fighting near Kohima was extremely close, but the larger campaign turned on roads, air supply, medical care, and the ability to replace losses. The Allied victory stopped the invasion and enabled a later advance into Burma. Remembering the campaign also means recognizing soldiers and civilians from many nations, not treating it as a story belonging to one country.
context: A multinational and logistics-centered account of the 1944 Imphal-Kohima campaign.
vocabulary: monsoon: a seasonal wind pattern bringing heavy rain
reinforcements: additional people or supplies sent to strengthen a force
source: Original summary based on Imperial War Museums, 10 Photos of the Battles of Imphal and Kohima
